stem_md: There are  $100$  cities in a country, some of them being joined by roads. Any four cities are connected to each other by at least two roads. Assume that there is no path passing through every city exactly once. Prove that there are two cities such that every other city is connected to at least one of them.
solution_md:
Consider the longest path  $v_1v_2 \cdots v_k$ , where  $k \le 99$  by the assumption that there is no Hamiltonian path. **Lemma 1.** If  $k \neq 99$ , the problem is true. **Proof.** Assume, for contradiction, that  $k \le 98.$  Let  $S$  be the set of vertices which aren't on the path. By assumption,  $|S| \ge 2.$  Call a vertex  $v_i$  on the path **social** if it is connected to at least vertex in  $S$ . Else, call  $v_i$  **antisocial**. Then, it's clear that for each  $1 \le i \le k-1$ , at least one of  $v_i, v_{i+1}$  is antisocial. Indeed, otherwise we could enlarge the path by travelling from  $v_1$  to  $v_i$ , then going from  $v_i$  to  $S$ , then exiting  $S$  to  $v_{i+1}$ , and finally travelling to  $v_k.$  Observe that both  $v_1$  and  $v_k$  must be antisocial, otherwise we can directly lengthen the path by adding an edge from  $v_1$  or  $v_k.$  Furthermore, observe that all antisocial vertices are connected to each other and all vertices in  $S$  are connected to each other, since if  $v_i, v_j$  are antisocial then we can apply the condition on  $v_i, v_j, a, b$  for  $a, b \in S$  (here we used  $|S| \ge 2$ ). If there are no social vertices, then our graph is simply the union of two complete graphs, and so we can satisfy the desired requirement by simply taking one city in each part. Otherwise, suppose that  $v_i$  is social, where  $i$  is the minimal such  $i$  with this holding. Then, if  $a$  is connected to  $v_i$  for  $a \in S$ , then  $av_iv_{i-1}v_{i-2} \cdots v_1 v_{i+1} v_{i+2} \cdots v_k$  is a longer path, where we used the fact that  $v_1 v_{i+1}$  is an edge since both are antisocial ( $v_{i+1}$  is because else  $v_i, v_{i+1}$  would both be social). This is a contradiction, and so the lemma is proven. $\blacksquare$  

As a result of the lemma, we need only to solve the problem when  $k = 99$ . Suppose that  $v_1 v_2 v_3 \cdots v_{99}$  is a path. Redefine  $S$  to be the other vertex which isn't on the path, say  $S = \{v\}$ . Again, call a vertex social if it is connected to  $v$  and antisocial otherwise. Observe that out of any three antisocial vertices, there must be at least two edges between them (just apply the condition on those three and  $v$ ). In particular, this means that each antisocial vertex  $w$  is connected with all other antisocial vertices, except possibly one. If there are no social vertices, then  $v$  has degree  $0$  and there are  $99$  antisocial vertices. It's well-known that there must be an antisocial vertex  $t$  with even degree, and so since all antisocial vertices have degree at least  $97$ , it must have degree  $98$ . In other words,  $t$  is connected to all antisocial vertices, and so the problem is solved by taking  $v$  and  $t$ . Otherwise, suppose that there exists some social vertex, say  $v_i$ . Again, observe that  $i \notin \{1, 99\}.$  Also, note that  $v_{i-1}, v_{i+1}$  must both be antisocial, else we can "insert"  $v$  into the path again. Note that we cannot possibly have that  $i-1 = 1$  and  $i+1 = 99$ , so WLOG assume that  $i-1 \neq 1$  by symmetry. Note that since  $v_{99}$  can only be disconnected with at most one other antisocial vertex, at least one of  $v_{i-1}v_{99}, v_1v_{99}$  is an edge. If  $v_{i-1} v_{99}$  is an edge, then the path  $v v_i v_{i+1} v_{i+2} \cdots v_{99} v_{i-1} v_{i-2} \cdots v_1$  is Hamiltonian, contradiction. If  $v_1v_{99}$  is an edge, then the path  $v v_i v_{i+1} \cdots v_{99} v_1 v_2 \cdots v_{i-1}$  is Hamiltonian, contradiction. Hence, there is no social vertex, and we're done in this case as well. $\square$

Since there is no edge between  $\{u,v\}$  and  $\{v_1,v_k\}$  we see that  $u,v$  are friends and  $v_1,v_k$  are friends. Thus, the longest path is a cycle. Let  $C$  be that cycle and the rest of the graph be  $A$ . Pick  $u,v\in A$  and two  $v_i,v_j\in C$ . We observe that  $v_i,v_j$  are friends hence both  $A,C$  are cliques which proves our result. Since any three vertices of that path must have at least two edges, anyone cannot have two "not friends". stem_md: Suppose that  $M$  is a set of  $2003$  numbers such that, for any distinct  $a, b \in M$ , the number  $a^2 +b\sqrt 2$  is rational. Prove that  $a\sqrt 2$  is rational for all  $a \in M.$
solution_md:
The set  $M$   is such that  $\forall_{a\neq b} (a^2+b\sqrt m )\in Q$  where  $m\in Q, \ m>0$  , and it  has at least 3 elements. Let  $a,b,c$  be 3 distinct elements .    $(c^2+a\sqrt m)\in Q,(c^2+b\sqrt m)\in Q)\Longrightarrow (a\sqrt m-b\sqrt m)\in Q$  $((a^2+b\sqrt m\in )\in Q,(b^2+a\sqrt m)\in Q) \Longrightarrow ((a\sqrt m)^2+mb\sqrt m)\in Q , $  $\ ((b\sqrt m)^2+ma\sqrt m)\in Q)$ Then we can write  $(a\sqrt m-b\sqrt m)(a\sqrt m+b\sqrt m) +m(b\sqrt m -a\sqrt m)))\in Q$  .
But  $m\in Q,(a\sqrt m-b\sqrt m)\in Q$  so  $(a\sqrt m+b\sqrt m)\in Q$  so  $(a\sqrt m-b\sqrt m)+(a\sqrt m+b\sqrt m)=2a\sqrt m \in Q$  and finaly  $a\sqrt m$  is rational.

stem_md: Two circles  $S_1$  and  $S_2$  with centers  $O_1$  and  $O_2$  respectively intersect at  $A$  and  $B$ . The tangents at  $A$  to  $S_1$  and  $S_2$  meet segments  $BO_2$  and  $BO_1$  at  $K$  and  $L$  respectively. Show that  $KL \parallel O_1O_2.$
solution_md: Let the line through  $K$  parallel to  $O_1O_2$  intersect  $O_1B$  at  $L'$ . Let  $\angle{AO_1B}=2x$ . Then we have that  $\angle{BAK}=x$ . Since  $O_1O_2$  bisects  $\angle{AO_1B}$ , we have that  $x=\angle{O_2O_1B}=\angle{KL'B}$ , hence  $AKL'B$  is cyclic. Now let  $\angle{O_1AL'}=y$ . Then  $90-x-y=\angle{L'AB}=\angle{L'KB}=\angle{O_1O_2B}$ . Let  $AK$  and  $O_1O_2$  intersect at  $T$ , we calculate  $\angle{ATO_2}=90+x$ , hence  $\angle{KAO_2}=y$ , so  $AL'$  and  $AK$  are isogonal, thus  $AL'$  is tangent to  $S_2$ , and  $L=L'$  as desired.  $\square$

stem_md: On a line are given  $2k -1$  white segments and  $2k -1$  black ones. Assume that each white segment intersects at least  $k$  black segments, and each black segment intersects at least  $k$  white ones. Prove that there are a black segment intersecting all the white ones, and a white segment intersecting all the black ones.
solution_md:
I'm not sure if the following works; if it does, this is way too simple for ARO. :maybe:

<details><summary> Solution</summary>I shall show that there must exist a white segment intersecting all black ones. Analogous arguments shall prove that there must exist a black segment intersecting all white ones. 

If there exists a white segment which intersects both the leftmost and the rightmost black segments, we're done. Assume otherwise. Since all black segments intersect at least  $k$  white segments and the set of white segments intersecting the leftmost black segment is disjoint with the set of white segments intersecting the rightmost black segment, the total number of white segments must be at least  $k+k=2k,$  contradiction.  $\blacksquare$</details>

Then, by the maximal principle for the last black, in order for it not have been placed in a way such that it must intersect all the whites, the leftmost white, Wi, must have had k-1 blacks intersecting it, and the rightmost white, Wf, must have had k-1 intersecting it as well. However, each white segment must be intersected by at least k blacks, so the last black segment must intersect Wi and Wl, causing it to intersect all the whites. The proof for the whites is similar. This is similar to spanferkel's idea but a bit shorter:

Let the white segments as in spanferkel's solution be  $W_1=[v_1,w_1],...,W_n=[v_n,w_n]$ . Now let  $W_i$  be such that  $w_i$  is minimal and  $W_j$  be such that  $v_j$  is maximal. 
By the pigeonhole principle, a black segment  $B = [a,b]$  must intersect both  $W_i$  and  $W_j$ . Now if  $B$  doesn't intersect  $W_k = [v_k,w_k]$ ,
then either  $b<v_k$  which means  $b<v_j$  (because  $v_j$  is maximal) contradiction. Or  $a>w_k$  which means  $a>w_i$  (because  $w_i$  is minimal) which is again a contradiction. 
Hence  $B$  intersects all white segments, and by symmetry there is a white segment intersecting all black segments.

stem_md: A sequence  $(a_n)$  is defined as follows:  $a_1 = p$  is a prime number with exactly  $300$  nonzero digits, and for each  $n \geq 1, a_{n+1}$  is the decimal period of  $1/a_n$  multiplies by  $2$ . Determine  $a_{2003}.$
solution_md:
I think the period here means the "repeating part," not its length. For instance,  $\frac17$  would have a period of  $142857$  and  $\frac13$  has a period of  $3$ .

<details><summary>Solution</summary>With this, the problem becomes pretty easy. The answer is  $\boxed{10p}.$  First, let's set out to find  $a_2$ . Let  $n$  be the order of  $10$  modulo  $p$ . Then, observe that  $\frac1p = \frac{\frac{10^n-1}{p}}{10^n-1}.$  Hence,  $\frac1p$  is just  $\frac{10^n-1}{p}$  repeated over and over again (padded with leading zeroes so as to have length  $n$ ). With this, we claim that  $\frac{10^n-1}{p}$  is the period of  $\frac1p.$  Indeed, suppose that the length of the period of  $\frac1p$  was actually  $m < n$ . This implies that  $(10^m-1) \cdot \frac1p$  is a terminating decimal. However, that cannot be, since  $p \nmid 10^m-1$  by the minimality of  $n$ , contradiction. Therefore,  $\frac{10^n-1}{p}$  is the period of  $\frac1p$ , so that  $a_2 = 2 \cdot \frac{10^n-1}{p}.$  Therefore, we've that  $a_3$  is double the period of   $$ \frac{p}{2(10^n-1)}. $$  This is also the period of  $\frac{5p}{10^n-1},$  since multiplying by  $10$  doesn't change the period (only shifts all digits to the left by  $1$ ). We claim that  $5p < 10^n-1$ . Indeed, since  $p | 10^n-1$ , if this were to be false then we would have that  $p = \frac{10^n-1}{x}$  for  $x \in \{1, 2, 3, 4\}$ , clearly absurd. Therefore, we have that  $\frac{5p}{10^n-1}$  is just  $5p$  repeated over and over (padded with leading zeroes if needed). Suppose, for contradiction, that  $n$  wasn't the length period. Then, we'd have that  $m < n$  is the length of the period, and so we similarly have that  $\frac{5p(10^m-1)}{10^n-1}$  is a terminating decimal. This therefore implies that  $10^n-1 | (10^m-1)p.$  Let  $d = \gcd(m, n)$ , so that  $\gcd(10^n-1, 10^m-1) = 10^d-1 \Rightarrow \frac{10^n-1}{10^d-1} | p.$  Hence, as  $\frac{10^n-1}{10^d-1} > 1$ , we must have that  $p (10^d-1) = 10^m-1.$  Observe that  $\frac{10^m-1}{10^d-1} = 10^{m-d} + 10^{m-2d} + \cdots + 10^d + 1$ , so from the condition that  $p$  has exactly  $300$  nonzero digits we know that  $m = 300d.$  Therefore, since  $v_3(10^{300d}-1) > v_3(10^d-1)$  by LTE, we've that  $3 | p$ , but this is clearly absurd since  $p$  is a prime larger than  $3$ . Hence, we've finally obtained our contradiction, and so the period of  $\frac{5p}{10^n-1}$  has length  $n$  and is just  $5p$ . This means that  $a_3 = 10p.$  

But wait, now we're happy, since  $q$  and  $\frac{q}{10}$  have the same periods for all rational  $q$ , and so therefore  $a_4 = a_2$ , hence making  $\{a_i\}$  periodic with minimal period exactly  $2$  :D (starting at  $a_2$ ). Therefore,  $a_{2003} = a_3 = 10p,$  as claimed.  $\square$</details>

stem_md: There are  $N$  cities in a country. Any two of them are connected either by a road or by an airway. A tourist wants to visit every city exactly once and return to the city at which he started the trip. Prove that he can choose a starting city and make a path, changing means of transportation at most once.
solution_md:
In graph theoretic language, we consider a two-coloring of  $K_n$  and the question is to show that there exists a Hamiltonian path, that is a union of a red path, and a blue path.

We will prove this via inducting on  $n$ . Assume the statement is true until and including  $(n-1)$ , now let us study  $n$ . Fix a vertex  $v$ , and consider the  $K_{n-1}$  obtained by removing  $v$  from the original  $K_n$ . By inductive hypothesis, this graph has a Hamiltonian cycle, which is a union of a blue and red paths. Without loss of generality, let  ${\rm BEGIN}$  be the node where the Hamiltonian starts,  $u$  is the node where  ${\rm BEGIN}-u$  is blue,  ${\rm LAST}$  be the last node, that is,  $u-{\rm LAST}$  is red, and also  ${\rm LAST}-{\rm BEGIN}$  edge is also red. Regarding the situtation of the edges connecting the removed vertex  $v$  to  $K_{n-1}$ , we divide the problem into four subcases. Let  $e_1$  be the edge connecting  $v$  to  $BEGIN$  and  $e_2$  be the edge connecting  $LAST$  to  $v$ . $1)$  If both  $e_1$  and  $e_2$  are blue, then start from LAST node, and consider the path,  $LAST-v-BEGIN-u$  which is blue. Now, we switch from  $u-LAST$  step to red, and conclude. $2)$ If  $e_1$  is blue and  $e_2$  is red, then  $v-BEGIN-u$  is a blue path, and  $u-END-v$  is the red path, concluding the proof. $3)$  Now suppose both  $e_1$  and  $e_2$  are red. Now, start from  $u$ , and trace the path  $u-LAST-v-BEGIN$ , which is all red. Now, at  $BEGIN$ , swap to blue path until  $u$ , closing the case. $4)$  In the last case, suppose that  $e_1$  is blue, and  $e_2$  is red. Now, let  $BEGIN_2$  be the neighbour of  $BEGIN$  along the blue path. Now, if  $v-BEGIN_2$  edge is blue, then take the path  $v-BEGIN_2-u$ , which is all blue, and then  $u-LAST-BEGIN_1-v$ , which is all red. Finally, if  $v-BEGIN_2$  is red then the path,  $BEGIN_2-v-BEGIN-LAST-u$  is a red path, and  $u-BEGIN_2$  is blue. We conclude.

stem_md:
Let  $a, b, c$  be positive numbers with the sum  $1$ . Prove the inequality
\[\frac{1}{1-a}+\frac{1}{1-b}+\frac{1}{1-c} \geq \frac{2}{1+a}+\frac{2}{1+b}+\frac{2}{1+c}.\]
solution_md: Let  $x=1-a$ . Define  $y$  and  $z$  similarly. It suffices to show that  $$ \frac{1}{x}+\frac{1}{y}+\frac{1}{z}\geq\frac{2}{2-x}+\frac{2}{2-y}+\frac{2}{2-z}=\frac{2}{x+y}+\frac{2}{y+z}+\frac{2}{x+z} $$   Note that  $$ \frac{1}{\sqrt{xy}}+\frac{1}{\sqrt{yz}}+\frac{1}{\sqrt{xz}}= \frac{2}{2\sqrt{xy}}+\frac{2}{2\sqrt{yz}}+\frac{2}{2\sqrt{xz}}\geq \frac{2}{x+y}+\frac{2}{y+z}+\frac{2}{x+z} $$  But  $$ \frac{1}{x}+\frac{1}{y}+\frac{1}{z}\geq \frac{1}{\sqrt{xy}}+\frac{1}{\sqrt{yz}}+\frac{1}{\sqrt{xz}} $$  follows directly from Cauchy, so we are done.  $\square$

stem_md: Is it possible to write a natural number in every cell of an infinite chessboard in such a manner that for all integers  $m, n > 100$ , the sum of numbers in every  $m\times n$  rectangle is divisible by  $m + n \ ?$
solution_md:
The answer is **no**.

To see why, consider some  $101\times 101$  square in this infinite grid. Then, pick a prime  $p>101$ . Consider the  $101p \times 101p$  square with the initially chosen  $101\times 101$  square as its top-right corner. Then, note that we can separate the  $101p\times 101p$  grid into  $p+1$  rectangles with size  $101 \times 101(p-1)$  stacked together along the left-side of the  $101p\times 101p$  square, and a single  $101 \times 101(p-1)$  rectangle placed lengthwise directly underneath the  $101 \times 101$  square. Note that this completely fills the  $101p\times 101p$  area. Further, let  $S_1$  be the sum of the elements in this square area and  $S_2$  be the sum of the numbers in the  $101p\times 101p$  square but not in the corner  $101\times 101$  grid. Then, clearly  $p \mid 202p \mid S_1$ . Further,  $p \mid 101p$  divides the sum of numbers in each  $101 \times 101(p-1)$  rectangle. So,  $p \mid S_2$ . Thus,  $p \mid S_1-S_2$  which implies that  $p$  divides the sum of the numbers in this  $101\times 101$  square for each prime  $p>101$  which is most clearly a contradiction implying that the answer is no as claimed.

stem_md: Let  $B$  and  $C$  be arbitrary points on sides  $AP$  and  $PD$  respectively of an acute triangle  $APD$ . The diagonals of the quadrilateral  $ABCD$  meet at  $Q$ , and  $H_1,H_2$  are the orthocenters of triangles  $APD$  and  $BPC$ , respectively. Prove that if the line  $H_1H_2$  passes through the intersection point  $X \ (X \neq Q)$  of the circumcircles of triangles  $ABQ$  and  $CDQ$ , then it also passes through the intersection point  $Y \  (Y \neq Q)$  of the circumcircles of triangles  $BCQ$  and  $ADQ.$
solution_md:
Let $B$ and $C$ be arbitrary points on sides $AP$ and $PD$ respectively of an acute triangle $APD$ . The diagonals of the quadrilateral $ABCD$ meet at $Q$ , and $H_1,H_2$ are the orthocenters of triangles $APD$ and $BPC$ , respectively. Prove that if the line $H_1H_2$ passes through the intersection point $X \ (X \neq Q)$ of the circumcircles of triangles $ABQ$ and $CDQ$ , then it also passes through the intersection point $Y \ (Y \neq Q)$ of the circumcircles of triangles $BCQ$ and $ADQ.$
Let $R=\overline{AD} \cap \overline{BC}$ . Suppose $\odot(AC), \odot(BD)$ meet at points $U, V$ . Line $\overline{UV}$ is their radical axis. By Gauss-Bodenmiller configuration, we know that $\overline{H_1H_2}$ is their radical axis; hence it coincides with $\overline{UV}$ . It is also well-known that $\odot(PR), \odot(AC), \odot(BD)$ are coaxial since their centers are collinear (Newton line), so $PUVR$ is cyclic. Thus, we want $X \in \overline{UV} \implies Y \in \overline{UV}$ . Invert at point $Q$ an denote images by $'$ s appended to them. Then we have $X'$ on the **cline** $QU'V'$ and we want $Y'$ to be on it too. We consider two cases:**1.** $ABCD$ is non-cyclic. Then $QB \cdot QD \ne QA \cdot QC$ hence $Q \not \in \overline{UV}$ so the cline is a circle. Note that $X'=\overline{A'B'} \cap \overline{C'D'}$ and $Y'=\overline{A'D'} \cap \overline{B'C'}$ . Thus, $U',V'$ lie on $\odot(X'Y')$ and so $X' \in \odot(QU'V') \implies X'Y'QU'V'$ is cyclic. Thus $Y' \in \odot(QU'V')$ and we're done. (Notice that $U', V'$ do not coincide with $X'$ since $\angle APD$ is acute.)**2.** $ABCD$ is cyclic. Then the cline is a line. Consequently, $X'$ has equal power in $\odot(A'C'), \odot(B'D')$ . However $X'B' \cdot X'A'=X'C' \cdot X'D'$ proving $X'A'=X'C'$ and $X'B'=X'D'$ . This is impossible and we get that the result is vacuously true in this case. Done. $\blacksquare$

Therefore we know that the triangles and congruent and so hence  $XM_1 = XM_2.$  As  $H_1H_2$  is the radical axis of the two circles and  $X$  is on it, we know that their radical axis is just the perpendicular bisector of  $M_1M_2.$  Hence, it simply suffices to observe that  $\triangle YBD \sim \triangle YCA \Rightarrow \triangle YBD \cong \triangle YCA \Rightarrow YM_1 = YM_2,$  so we're done since  $Y$  lies on the radical axis of the two circles as well. $\square$

stem_md: Suppose that  $M$  is a set of  $2003$  numbers such that, for any distinct  $a, b, c \in M$ , the number  $a^2 + bc$  is rational. Prove that there is a positive integer  $n$  such that  $a\sqrt n$  is rational for all  $a \in M.$
solution_md:
The following solution was communicated to me by [Applepi2000](http://www.artofproblemsolving.com/Forum/memberlist.php?mode=viewprofile&u=82357)
Here is my solution to this problem:
SolutionLet $a, b, c, d$ be arbitrary numbers in $M$ . Note that: \[(d^2+ac)-(d^2+bc)=c(a-b)\in\mathbb{Q}\] \[(a^2+bc)-(b^2+ac)=(a-b)(a+b-c)\in\mathbb{Q}\] \[\frac{(a+b-c)(a-b)}{c(a-b)}+2=\frac{a+b+c}{c}\in\mathbb{Q}\] Similarly, \[\frac{a+b+c}{b}\in\mathbb{Q}\implies\frac{\frac{a+b+c}{c}}{\frac{a+b+c}{b}}=\frac{b}{c}\in\mathbb{Q}\] Since $b, c$ were arbitrary, this means $\frac{x}{y}\in\mathbb{Q}\forall x, y\in M$ . This means that there exists a constant $\alpha$ such that $x\alpha\in\mathbb{Q}\forall x\in M$ . Now we know $(a\alpha)^2+(b\alpha)(c\alpha)=(\alpha^2)(a^2+bc)\in\mathbb{Q}$ , so $\alpha^2\in\mathbb{Q}$ . Now let $\alpha^2=\frac{n}{m}$ and let $M=\{a_1, a_2, \cdots, a_{2003}\}$ . Let $a_i\alpha=\frac{n_i}{m_i}$ . Then note that: \[a_i=\sqrt{\frac{m}{n}}\frac{n_i}{m_i}\] So $a_i\sqrt{mn}=\frac{mn_i}{m_i}$ is rational for all $a_i$ . We're done. $\blacksquare$

stem_md: In a triangle  $ABC, O$  is the circumcenter and  $I$  the incenter. The excircle  $\omega_a$  touches rays  $AB,AC$  and side  $BC$  at  $K,M,N$ , respectively. Prove that if the midpoint  $P$  of  $KM$  lies on the circumcircle of  $\triangle ABC$ , then points  $O,N, I$  lie on a line.
solution_md: Here is a completely synthetic solution. Rename $N,M,K$ with $D,E,F$ respectively because personal preferences. If $AB=AC$ , the result is obvious. Thus assume that $AB\ne AC$ . Let $M$ be the midpoint of $EF$ and $A'$ be the $A$ -antipode of $\triangle ABC$ . Obviously $A,I,M$ are colinear. Now since $ME=MF$ , we can construct point $C'$ such that $\triangle MC'F$ is directly congruent to $\triangle MCE$ . This gives $$ \measuredangle MBF = \measuredangle MBA = \measuredangle MCA = \measuredangle MCE = \measuredangle MC'F \implies MBFC'\text{ concyclic}. $$ Moreover $\angle BC'F = \angle BMF = 90^{\circ}-\angle AMB = 90^{\circ}-\angle C$ and analogously $\angle C'BF = 90^{\circ}-\angle B$ which means $\triangle BFC'\sim\triangle BA'C$ or $$ \frac{BA'}{A'C} = \frac{BF}{FC'} = \frac{BF}{CE} = \frac{BD}{DC} $$ or $A'D$ pass through midpoint $N$ of arc $BAC$ . Now let $I_A$ be the $A$ -excenter and $J$ be the Bevan point (reflection of $\small{I}$ across $\small{O}$ ) of $\triangle ABC$ . Since $M$ is the midpoint of $II_A$ , we get $I_AJ\perp BC$ or $J\in I_AD$ . Moreover, observe that $A'J\parallel AI\parallel A'N$ thus $J\in A'D$ . As $AB\ne AC$ , this forces $D=J$ so done.

stem_md: Find the greatest natural number  $N$  such that, for any arrangement of the numbers  $1, 2, \ldots, 400$  in a chessboard  $20 \times 20$ , there exist two numbers in the same row or column, which differ by at least  $N.$
solution_md: I found the answer  $209$ . $Lemma:$  For any arrangement, there exist two numbers  $a,b$  on the same row or column such that  $\mid a-b\mid =209$ . $Proof$   $of$   $the$   $lemma:$  Let  $S=\{1,2,\ldots ,400\},A=\{1,2,\ldots ,91\},B=\{300,301,\ldots ,400\}$ . For a subset  $X$  of  $S$ , let  $R_X$  is the set of all rows which each of them has an element from  $X$ , and let  $C_X$  is the set of all columns which each of them has an element from  $X$ . For any two sets  $Y,Z;Y\subset {R_S},Z\subset {C_S}$ , let  $T_{Y,Z}$  is the set such that  $n\in T_{Y,Z}\iff n\in S$  and  $n$  is on the intersection of a row  $r_i$  and a column  $c_j$  such that  $r_i\in Y,c_j\in Z$ . Then  $\mid T_{Y,Z}\mid =\mid Y\mid \mid Z\mid$  and  $X\subset T_{{R_X},{C_X}}$ . Thus  $\mid T_{{R_X},{C_X}}\mid =\mid R_X\mid \mid C_X\mid \geq \mid X\mid$ . Let  ${R_X}'=R_S/R_X$  and  ${C_X}'=C_S/C_X$ . Then if  $R_B$  is not a subset of  ${R_A}'$  or  $C_B$  is not a subset of  ${C_A}'$ , then  ${R_B}\cap {R_A}\neq \emptyset$  or  ${C_B}\cap {C_A}\neq \emptyset$ . So there will be a pair  $(a,b)$  such that  $a\in A,b\in B$ , and  $a$  and  $b$  are on same row or column. Since  $\mid a-b\mid \geq 300-91=209$ ,we're done, so suppose the contrary. Then  $T_{{R_B},{C_B}}\subset T_{{R_A}',{C_A}'}$ . Then  $\mid  T_{{R_A}',{C_A}'}\mid \geq \mid T_{{R_B},{C_B}} \mid$ . Now we can say that  $\mid T_{{R_A},{C_A}}\mid =\mid R_A\mid \mid C_A\mid \geq \mid A\mid =91$ ,  $\mid T_{{R_A}',{C_A}'}\mid =\mid {R_A}'\mid \mid {C_A}'\mid =(20-\mid R_A\mid )(20-\mid C_A\mid )\geq  \mid T_{{R_B},{C_B}}\mid =\mid R_B\mid \mid C_B\mid \geq \mid B\mid =101.$ If  $\mid R_A\mid \geq 15$  then  $\mid R_B\mid \leq \mid {R_A}'\mid =20-\mid R_A\mid \leq 5$ , and since  $\mid C_B\mid \leq 20$ ;  $\mid T_{{R_B},{C_B}}\mid =\mid R_B\mid \mid C_B\mid \leq 100$  which is a contradiction, so  $\mid R_A\mid \leq 14$ , so by symmetry,  $\mid C_A\mid \leq 14$ . Wlog we can assume that  $\mid R_A\mid \geq \mid C_A\mid$ . Then  $\mid R_A\mid \geq \sqrt{91}$  so  $\mid R_A\mid \geq 10$ . For a number  $k$ , if  $14\geq k\geq 10$  and  $\mid R_A\mid \geq k$  then  $20-\mid R_A\mid \leq 20-k$  so  $20-\mid C_A\mid \geq \lceil \frac{101}{20-k}\rceil$  so  $\mid C_A\mid \leq 20-\lceil \frac{101}{20-k}\rceil$  so  $\mid R_A\mid \geq \lceil \frac{91}{20-\lceil \frac{101}{20-k}\rceil}\rceil =f(k)$ . Since  $\mid R_A\mid \geq 10$ ;  $\mid R_A\mid \geq f(10)=11$ ,so  $\mid R_A\mid \geq f(11)=12$ , so  $\mid R_A\mid \geq f(12)=13$ , so  $\mid R_A\mid \geq f(13)=19$ , but this contradicts with  $\mid R_A\mid \leq 14$ . This completes the proof of the lemma.  $\Box$  On the other hand, for the arrangement which  $i$ 'th row's values from left to right are  $\{1+10(i-1),2+10(i-1),\ldots ,10+10(i-1),201+10(i-1),202+10(i-1),\ldots ,210+10(i-1)\},$ for each two numbers from same row or same column, their distance is less than  $210$ . So the answer is  $209$ .

In your case, $k=10$ , hence $N=209$ , making the above answer correct.

Let there be  $n$  rows and  $n$  columns, with  $n$  even. If an arrangement has maximum row/column difference  $k$ , we can transform it into another one such that every row from left to right and column from top to bottom is in increasing order. We do this by first moving the minimum of each row and each column to the leftmost column and topmost row, respectively. Then, we have an  $n-2$  by  $n-2$  empty square, and we repeat until there are no squares left. 

Thus we only have to consider cases where the rows and columns are sorted. We construct such a configuration by noting that 1 goes in the top left and  $n^2$  in the lower right. Then, we add A = {2,3...} and  B= { $n^2 -1$ ,  $n^2-2$ , ...}  by noting that there cannot be any blank squares to the left or above numbers in A, and there cannot be numbers below or to the right of numbers in B. Thus, it forms sort of 2 closed polygons, which must eventually both cross some row/column. The most squares that there can be filled in before this intersecting happens is  $a(b) + (n-a)(n-b)$  (2 rectangles sharing a vertex) whose maximal value is  $\frac{n^2}{2}$ . Through some smoothing arguments (too lazy to put into words, it's pretty simple), we know that the difference between the minimal row/column is at least  $\frac{n(n+1)}{2} -1$ . We can construct such a case in many ways, so it is indeed the greatest guaranteed difference.  $n=20$  yields  $209$ .

<details><summary>solution</summary>In general, we show that for a  $2n \times 2n$  the required value of  $N$  is  $2n^2+n-1$ . In particular, the answer for a  $20 \times 20$  board is  $209$ .

For the construction, we divide the  $2n \times 2n$  board into a  $2 \times 2$  square. In each of the  $n \times n$  subboards we fill in an interval of numbers  $[kn^2+1, (k+1)n^2]$  for  $0 \leq k \leq 3$  so that the subboards for  $k = 0$  and  $k = 4$  are NOT adjacent. It's easy to see that this ensures that the maximum value of the difference of two numbers in the same row of column is  $2n^2+n-1$ .

Now let us prove the bound. We first place a strawberry on each cell containing a number at most  $n^2$ . Observe that this means there are exactly  $n^2$  strawberries. Let  $\mathcal C$  denote the set of cells  $c$  of the board such that there is a strawberry in either  $c$ 's row or column (it is allowed for  $c$  to contain the strawberry).  Observe that  $\mathcal C$  is a union of some rows and some columns. Suppose there are  $a$  rows and  $b$  columns. We note two things:


- $|\mathcal C| = 2n(a+b)-ab$ : this is easily seen.
- $ab \geq n^2$ : To prove this, we note that strawberries appear in  $\mathcal C$  only at the intersections of one of the  $a$  rows and one of the  $b$  columns. Since there are  $n^2$  strawberries, this proves the bound.
[/list]
There are two cases: 
[list]
- $a = b= n$ : This case is easy to deal with. We have  $|\mathcal C| = 3n^2$ , so there is some cell  $c \in \mathcal C$  such that  $c$  has a number  $\geq 3n^2$  written on it. Pick such a cell  $c$  and consider the row or column from which it was added to  $\mathcal C$ . This contains exactly  $n$  numbers  $\leq n^2$ ; one of them is  $\leq n^2-n+1$ . In particular, the difference between the number in cell  $c$  and that other cell is at least  $2n^2+n-1$ , as needed.
- $a \ne b$ : Without losing generality, we may assume  $a > b$ . Clearly  $a > n$ , let us write  $a = n+u$  for some positive integer  $u$ . Since  $ab \geq n^2$  by say AM-GM, we have  $a+b \geq 2n+1$ . Thus we obtain  $b \geq n-u+1$ . So \[|\mathcal C| = 2n(a+b)-ab = 2n(n+u) + (2n-a)b \geq 2n^2+2nu+(n-u)^2+n-u = 3n^2+n+(u^2-u) \geq 3n^2+n\]
Thus there is a cell  $c$  in  $\mathcal C$  with a number  $\geq 3n^2+n$  written on it. Picking this cell and any strawberry cell in the same row or column as the chosen cell (which exists by definition), we ensure a difference of  $\geq 3n^2+n-n^2 \geq 2n^2+n-1$ , as needed.

With the above two cases, we deduce that there are two cells with a difference of  $\geq 2n^2+n-1$ . Since it was proven we cannot do better, this is our desired answer.  $\square$</details>

Prove that \[\sqrt{n-1}\left(x_1^2+x_2^2+\dots+x_n^2\right)\geq 2S.\]

solution_md: Nice problem, although the source doesn't look correct. These olympiads have several rounds; unless you are talking about the final round, you should mention which one it is from. **Problem.** Let $G$ be a tree with $n\geq 2$ vertices. Let $x_v$ be a real number for every $v\in V\left(G\right)$ . For every edge $e$ of $G$ , let $s\left(e\right)$ denote one of the endpoints of $e$ (arbitrarily chosen), and let $t\left(e\right)$ denote the other endpoint of $e$ . Prove that $\sqrt{n-1}\sum_{v\in V\left(G\right)} x_v^2 \geq 2\sum_{e\in E\left(G\right)} x_{s\left(e\right)}x_{t\left(e\right)}$ . *Solution (sketched).* We will solve this problem by induction over $n$ . The induction base case ( $n=2$ ) is equivalent to the well-known inequality $a^2+b^2\geq 2ab$ for any two reals $a$ and $b$ . Thus, it is clearly true. Now to the induction step: Let $n\geq 3$ be some integer. Assume that the problem is already solved for $n-1$ instead of $n$ . Let us solve it for $n$ now: Let $G$ be a tree with $n$ vertices. We WLOG assume that all of the reals $x_v$ are nonnegative. (Otherwise, we simply replace each $x_v$ by the respective $\left|x_v\right|$ . This only makes the inequality sharper, as the left hand side ( $\sqrt{n-1}\sum_{v\in V\left(G\right)} x_v^2$ ) does not change, while the right hand side ( $2\sum_{e\in E\left(G\right)} x_{s\left(e\right)}x_{t\left(e\right)}$ ) increases.) It is known that for every graph $H$ , the sum of the degrees of all vertices of $H$ is twice the number of edges of $H$ . Applying this to $H=G$ and recalling that the number of edges of $G$ is $n-1$ (since $G$ is a tree on $n$ vertices), we see that the sum of the degrees of all vertices of $G$ is $2\left(n-1\right)$ . Hence, at least one vertex of $G$ has degree $\leq 1$ (because otherwise, every vertex of $G$ would have degree $\geq 2$ , so that the sum of the degrees of all vertices of $G$ would be $\geq 2n$ , contradicting to the fact that this sum is $2\left(n-1\right)$ ). Let $a$ be such a vertex. Then, the degree of $a$ is $\leq 1$ . Since the degree of $a$ cannot be zero (because $G$ is a tree with $n\geq 3$ vertices, and a tree with more than $1$ vertex cannot have isolated vertices), this yields that the degree of $a$ is $1$ . In other words, the vertex $a$ has exactly one neighbour in $G$ . Denote this neighbour by $b$ . Let $G'$ be the tree obtained from $G$ by removing the vertex $a$ and the edge $ab$ . Then, $G'$ has $n-1$ vertices. For every $v\in V\left(G'\right)$ , define a real $y_v$ as follows: $y_v = \left\{ \begin{array}{c} \sqrt{\frac{n-2}{n-1}} x_v\text{, if }v=b; x_v\text{, if }v\neq b \end{array}\right.$ . Since $n-1\geq 2$ (because $n\geq 3$ ), we can apply the problem to the integer $n-1$ , the tree $G'$ and the numbers $y_v$ instead of the integer $n$ , the tree $G$ and the numbers $x_v$ (because we assumed that the problem is already solved for $n-1$ instead of $n$ ), and we obtain **(1)** $\sqrt{\left(n-1\right)-1}\sum_{v\in V\left(G'\right)} y_v^2 \geq 2\sum_{e\in E\left(G'\right)} y_{s\left(e\right)}y_{t\left(e\right)}$ . Let us WLOG assume that every edge $e$ of $G$ such that $b\in e$ satisfies $t\left(e\right)=b$ and $s\left(e\right)\neq b$ . (Otherwise, we can simply switch $s\left(e\right)$ with $t\left(e\right)$ ; this clearly doesn't change anything.) Then, every edge $e$ of $G$ such that $b\in e$ satisfies $y_{s\left(e\right)}=x_{s\left(e\right)}$ (by the definition of $y_{s\left(e\right)}$ , since $s\left(e\right)\neq b$ ) and $y_{t\left(e\right)} = \sqrt{\frac{n-2}{n-1}} x_{t\left(e\right)}$ (by the definition of $y_{t\left(e\right)}$ , since $t\left(e\right)=b$ ). Hence, every edge $e$ of $G$ such that $b\in e$ satisfies $y_{s\left(e\right)}y_{t\left(e\right)} = x_{s\left(e\right)}\cdot \sqrt{\frac{n-2}{n-1}} x_{t\left(e\right)} = \sqrt{\frac{n-2}{n-1}}x_{s\left(e\right)}x_{t\left(e\right)}$ . Note that $t\left(ab\right)=b$ (since every edge $e$ of $G$ such that $b\in e$ satisfies $t\left(e\right)=b$ ), so that $s\left(ab\right)$ must be the endpoint of the edge $ab$ other than $b$ . In other words, $s\left(ab\right)=a$ . Hence, $x_{s\left(ab\right)}x_{t\left(ab\right)}=x_ax_b$ . On the other hand, every edge $e$ of $G$ such that $b\notin e$ satisfies $t\left(e\right)\neq b$ and $s\left(e\right)\neq b$ . Hence, every edge $e$ of $G$ such that $b\notin e$ satisfies $y_{s\left(e\right)}=x_{s\left(e\right)}$ (by the definition of $y_{s\left(e\right)}$ , since $s\left(e\right)\neq b$ ) and $y_{t\left(e\right)} = x_{t\left(e\right)}$ (by the definition of $y_{t\left(e\right)}$ , since $t\left(e\right)\neq b$ ). Hence, every edge $e$ of $G$ such that $b\notin e$ satisfies $y_{s\left(e\right)}y_{t\left(e\right)} = x_{s\left(e\right)}x_{t\left(e\right)}$ . We have $\left(n-1\right)-1=n-2$ and $\sum_{v\in V\left(G'\right)} y_v^2 = \sum_{v\in V\left(G'\right)} \left(\left\{ \begin{array}{c} \sqrt{\frac{n-2}{n-1}} x_v\text{, if }v=b; x_v\text{, if }v\neq b \end{array}\right.\right)^2$ (by the definition of $y_v$ ) $= \left(\sqrt{\frac{n-2}{n-1}}x_b\right)^2 + \sum_{v\in V\left(G'\right);\ v\neq b} x_v^2 = \frac{n-2}{n-1} x_b^2 + \sum_{v\in V\left(G'\right);\ v\neq b} x_v^2$ and $\sum_{e\in E\left(G'\right)} y_{s\left(e\right)}y_{t\left(e\right)} = \sum_{e\in E\left(G'\right);\ b\in e} \underbrace{y_{s\left(e\right)}y_{t\left(e\right)}}_{=\sqrt{\frac{n-2}{n-1}}x_{s\left(e\right)}x_{t\left(e\right)}} + \sum_{e\in E\left(G'\right);\ b\notin e} \underbrace{y_{s\left(e\right)}y_{t\left(e\right)}}_{=x_{s\left(e\right)}x_{t\left(e\right)}\geq \sqrt{\frac{n-2}{n-1}}x_{s\left(e\right)}x_{t\left(e\right)}}$ $\geq \sum_{e\in E\left(G'\right);\ b\in e} \sqrt{\frac{n-2}{n-1}}x_{s\left(e\right)}x_{t\left(e\right)} + \sum_{e\in E\left(G'\right);\ b\notin e} \sqrt{\frac{n-2}{n-1}}x_{s\left(e\right)}x_{t\left(e\right)}$ $= \sum_{e\in E\left(G'\right)} \sqrt{\frac{n-2}{n-1}}x_{s\left(e\right)}x_{t\left(e\right)} = \sqrt{\frac{n-2}{n-1}} \sum_{e\in E\left(G'\right)} x_{s\left(e\right)}x_{t\left(e\right)}$ . These three computations transform **(1)** into $\sqrt{n-2} \left(\frac{n-2}{n-1} x_b^2 + \sum_{v\in V\left(G'\right);\ v\neq b} x_v^2\right) \geq 2\sqrt{\frac{n-2}{n-1}} \sum_{e\in E\left(G'\right)} x_{s\left(e\right)}x_{t\left(e\right)}$ . Dividing both sides of this inequality by $\sqrt{n-2}$ , we obtain $\frac{n-2}{n-1} x_b^2 + \sum_{v\in V\left(G'\right);\ v\neq b} x_v^2 \geq \frac{2}{\sqrt{n-1}} \sum_{e\in E\left(G'\right)} x_{s\left(e\right)}x_{t\left(e\right)}$ . Now, let us add this inequality to the inequality $x_a^2 + \frac{1}{n-1} x_b^2 \geq \frac{2}{\sqrt{n-1}}x_ax_b$ (which follows trivially from $x_a^2 + \frac{1}{n-1} x_b^2 - \frac{2}{\sqrt{n-1}}x_ax_b = \left(x_a - \frac{1}{\sqrt{n-1}} x_b\right)^2 \geq 0$ ). We obtain $x_a^2 + \frac{1}{n-1} x_b^2 + \frac{n-2}{n-1} x_b^2 + \sum_{v\in V\left(G'\right);\ v\neq b} x_v^2 $ $\geq \frac{2}{\sqrt{n-1}}x_ax_b + \frac{2}{\sqrt{n-1}} \sum_{e\in E\left(G'\right)} x_{s\left(e\right)}x_{t\left(e\right)}$ . Since $x_a^2 + \underbrace{\frac{1}{n-1} x_b^2 + \frac{n-2}{n-1} x_b^2}_{=x_b^2} + \sum_{v\in V\left(G'\right);\ v\neq b} x_v^2 = x_a^2 + x_b^2 + \sum_{v\in V\left(G'\right);\ v\neq b} x_v^2$ $= x_a^2 + \sum_{v\in V\left(G'\right)} x_v^2 $ (since $x_b^2 + \sum_{v\in V\left(G'\right);\ v\neq b} x_v^2 = \sum_{v\in V\left(G'\right)} x_v^2 $ ) $= \sum_{v\in V\left(G\right)} x_v^2$ (since $V\left(G'\right)=V\left(G\right)\setminus \left\{a\right\}$ by the definition of $G'$ ) and $\frac{2}{\sqrt{n-1}}x_ax_b + \frac{2}{\sqrt{n-1}} \sum_{e\in E\left(G'\right)} x_{s\left(e\right)}x_{t\left(e\right)} = \frac{2}{\sqrt{n-1}} \left( \underbrace{x_ax_b}_{=x_{s\left(ab\right)}x_{t\left(ab\right)}} + \sum_{e\in E\left(G'\right)} x_{s\left(e\right)}x_{t\left(e\right)}\right)$ $= \frac{2}{\sqrt{n-1}} \underbrace{\left( x_{s\left(ab\right)}x_{t\left(ab\right)} + \sum_{e\in E\left(G'\right)} x_{s\left(e\right)}x_{t\left(e\right)}\right)}_{=\sum\limits_{e\in E\left(G\right)} x_{s\left(e\right)}x_{t\left(e\right)}\text{ (since }E\left(G'\right)=E\left(G\right)\setminus \left\{ab\right\}\text{ by the definition of }G'\text{)}}$ $= \frac{2}{\sqrt{n-1}} \sum_{e\in E\left(G\right)} x_{s\left(e\right)}x_{t\left(e\right)}$ , this simplifies to $\sum_{v\in V\left(G\right)} x_v^2 \geq \frac{2}{\sqrt{n-1}} \sum_{e\in E\left(G\right)} x_{s\left(e\right)}x_{t\left(e\right)}$ . In other words, $\sqrt{n-1}\sum_{v\in V\left(G\right)} x_v^2 \geq 2\sum_{e\in E\left(G\right)} x_{s\left(e\right)}x_{t\left(e\right)}$ . Thus, the problem is solved for our $n$ . This completes the induction step. So the problem is really solved now. This was written in a hurry. Sorry for the inevitable mistakes.

Let  $e_{ij}$  be the edge connecting vertices with numbers  $x_i$  and  $x_j$ . Denote  $n_i\left(e_{ij}\right)$  the number of vertices that would not be connected by a path to vertex  $x_i$  if the edge were removed.
Then \[1\leq n_i\left(e_{ij}\right),n_j\left(e_{ij}\right)\leq n-1,\]
\[n_i\left(e_{ij}\right)+n_j\left(e_{ij}\right)=n.\]
Also, since the graph is a tree, it is possible to find unique path without cycles from vertex  $x_i$  to any of the remaining  $n-1$  vertices, we have \[\sum_{\textrm{all vertices\, }j \textrm{\, connected to\, } x_i} n_i\left(e_{ij}\right)=n-1.\]
By AM-GM inequality
\[\frac{n_i\left(e_{ij}\right)}{\sqrt{n-1}}x_i^2+\frac{n_j\left(e_{ij}\right)}{\sqrt{n-1}}x_j^2\geq 2\sqrt{\frac{n_i\left(e_{ij}\right)n_j\left(e_{ij}\right)}{n-1}}|x_ix_j|\geq 2x_ix_j,\]
where the last inequality follows from
\[n_i\left(e_{ij}\right)n_j\left(e_{ij}\right)=\frac{\left(n_i\left(e_{ij}\right)+n_j\left(e_{ij}\right)\right)^2-\left(n_i\left(e_{ij}\right)-n_j\left(e_{ij}\right)\right)^2}{4}\geq\frac{n^2-\left(\left(n-1\right)-1\right)^2}{4}=n-1.\]

The last step is to add such inequalities for all edges  $e_{ij}$ .

A nice idea indeed, but it needs a little bit more explanation. First we can assume that all real numbers $x_i$ are non negative, because if the inequality is true for non negative numbers, it will be true for any reals. Some notations. Given graph $G$ , with assigned real numbers $x_v, \forall v\in V(G)$ . Let for every edge $e \in E(G)$ , $r(e)$ means endpoint of $e$ which is nearer to the root of $G$ , $l(e)$ means the other vertex, nearer to the leaves of the graph. Let $S_2(G) = \sqrt{n-1} \sum_{v\in V(G)} x_v^2 \,,\, S(G) = 2 \sum_{e \in E(G)} v_{r(e)} v_{l(e)}$ . We must prove: (1) $ S_2(G) \geq S(G) $ . Let $u \in V(G),\, x_u = \max_{v \in V(G)} x_v $ . Assign $u$ to be the root of the tree $G$ . The main idea is to construct a new graph $G'$ which is more simple than $G$ and $S_{2}(G)=S_2(G'),\, S(G') \geq S(G)$ . So it will be enough to prove (1) for $G'$ and then it will be true also for $G$ . But because $G'$ is simplier it is easy to check (1). Let $G'$ consists of the same vertices as $G$ , $V(G')= V(G)$ and $E(G') = \left\{uv\,|\, v \in V(G)-\{u\} \right\} $ If $E(G') \ni e'= uv $ and $e \in E(G), \, l(e) = v$ then $x_u x_v \geq x_{r(e)} x_v$ . Hence: $S(G') \geq S(G)$ and obviously $S_2(G') = S_2(G)$ . But $G'$ is a very simple tree which consists of a vertex connected with all other vertices and (1) is very easily checked, as it is done in the above post of Merlinaeus. EDIT: some LaTeX improved.

WLOG assume that  $x_1$  is the largest real number assigned. Then reassigning all edges to pass through  $v_1$  makes the left side of the equation constant while the right side increases. 

Therefore, it suffices to show that  $\sqrt {n-1} (x_1^2 + x_2^2 + \cdots + x_n^2) \ge 2 x_1 (x_2 + x_3 + \cdots + x_n)$ . 

From AM-GM,  $\dfrac {x_1^2} {\sqrt {n - 1}} + x_i^2\sqrt {n - 1} \ge 2 x_1 x_i$  for all  $2 \le i \le n$ . 

Summing each individual inequality, we get   $\sqrt {n-1} (x_1^2 + x_2^2 + \cdots + x_n^2) \ge 2 x_1 (x_2 + x_3 + \cdots + x_n)$ , as desired.

<details><summary>sol</summary>Firstly, note that changing  $x_i \rightarrow |x_i|$  does not affect the left side but may increase the right one, so it is sufficient to show the result when all numbers are non negative. Note that any tree on  $n$  vertices has exactly  $n-1$  edges. A tree is called a *capitalist* tree if there exists a vertex connected to all others by an edge. 

I shall prove the result for all *capitalist* trees before proving the general case. Indeed, we want   $$ \sqrt{n-1}\left(x_1^2+\dots+x_n^2\right) \ge 2x_1\left(x_2+\dots+x_n\right), $$   which can be viewed as a quadratic in  $x_1 \ge 0$ . It's leading coefficient is positive and it's discriminant is given by   $$ (x_2+\dots+x_n)^2-(n-1)(x_2^2+\dots+x_n^2) \le 0, $$   where the last inequality is just Cauchy Schwartz, so the result holds.

For  $n=2$  the result is clear and for  $n=3$  we know that any tree is a capitalist. Proceed by induction on  $n \ge 4$ . Let the result hold for all  $k \le n$ . I will show that it works for  $k=n+1$  as well.

Note that for any non-capitalist tree on  $n \ge 4$  vertices, the maximal path has length at least three. Indeed, pick a vertex  $v$  of maximal degree and a vertex  $w$  not adjacent to it. If the maximal path has length  $\le 2$  then there exists  $u$  adjacent to  $v$  and  $w$ . Since  $\text{deg}(v)  \ge \text{deg}(u) \ge 2,$  we have a vertex  $x$  adjacent to  $v$  with  $x \notin \{u, w\},$  so  $wuvx$  is a path of length three, a contradiction!

It is also clear that the endpoints of a maximal path are vertices with degree one, otherwise, we can either append one of their neighbors to get a longer path, or obtain a cycle, both of which are impossible. Let this path be labelled  $v_iv_{i+1}\dots v_{j-1}v_j$ . WLOG, let  $x_{i+1} \le x_{j-1}$  and by the induction hypothesis, we get   $$ 2S \le 2x_ix_{i+1}+\sqrt{n-1}\sum_{k \ne i, k \le n} x_k^2, $$   so it is sufficient to show   $$ 2x_ix_{i+1} \le \sqrt{n}x_i^2+\left(\sqrt{n}-\sqrt{n-1}\right)\sum_{k \ne i, k \le n+1} x_k^2 \Longleftarrow 2\left(\sqrt{n}-\sqrt{n-1}\right)x_{i+1}^2+\sqrt{n}x_i^2 \ge 2x_ix_{i+1}, $$   where the last implication is true because  $x_{j-1} \ge x_{i+1}$  and  $j-1 \ne i+1$ . Evidently, letting  $\frac{x_i}{x_{i+1}}=t$  the last implication is equivalent to proving the quadratic inequality   $$ \sqrt{n}t^2-2t+2\left(\sqrt{n}-\sqrt{n-1}\right) \ge 0. $$   It is clear that the leading coefficient of this quadratic trinomial is positive and as the discriminant  $D$  satisfies   $$ D=4\left(1-2\sqrt{n}\left(\sqrt{n}-\sqrt{n-1}\right)\right)=4\left(1-\frac{2\sqrt{n}}{\sqrt{n}+\sqrt{n-1}}\right)<0, $$   we are done!</details>

A tree with $n\geq 2$ vertices is given. (A tree is a connected graph without cycles.) The vertices of the tree have real numbers $x_1,x_2,\dots,x_n$ associated with them. Each edge is associated with the product of the two numbers corresponding to the vertices it connects. Let $S$ be a sum of number across all edges. Prove that \[\sqrt{n-1}\left(x_1^2+x_2^2+\dots+x_n^2\right)\geq 2S.\] *(Author: V. Dolnikov)*
**Solution.** Let the given tree be $T(V,E)$ with the vertices $v_1,v_2,v_3,\ldots,v_n,$ where $\delta(v_i)$ is assigned to $v_i.$ Note that if we delete an edge from $T$ , the graph gets disconnected. For two adjacent vertices $v_i$ and $v_j,$ define $\Delta_{v_i}(v_j)$ as - First delete the edge between $v_i$ and $v_j $ so that $T$ splits into two disconnected trees. - Now $\Delta_{v_i}(v_j)$ is the number of vertices in the tree which doesn't contain $v_j.$ For example in the following tree, $\Delta_{v_1}(v_3)=1$ and $\Delta_{v_4}(v_3)=2.$ [asy] import graph; size(10cm); real labelscalefactor = 0.5; pen dps = linewidth(0.7) + fontsize(10); defaultpen(dps); pen dotstyle = black; real xmin = -5.251571738656087, xmax = 4.736141353206572, ymin = -3.13207380918071, ymax = 3.8143979259902; draw((-4.66,1.8)--(-2.88,0.42), linewidth(0.8)); draw((-2.88,0.42)--(-4.88,-1.44), linewidth(0.8)); draw((-2.88,0.42)--(0.24339843991195068,0.4621205214549849), linewidth(0.8)); draw((0.24339843991195068,0.4621205214549849)--(2.558889018302256,0.660837996466093), linewidth(0.8)); dot((-4.66,1.8),dotstyle); label(" $v_1$ ", (-4.629499642969139,1.8877024074042388), NE * labelscalefactor); dot((-2.88,0.42),dotstyle); label(" $v_3$ ", (-2.8496822580870393,0.5053199725443562), NE * labelscalefactor); dot((-4.88,-1.44),dotstyle); label(" $v_2$ ", (-4.8454968984159965,-1.352256424298611), NE * labelscalefactor); dot((0.24339843991195068,0.4621205214549849),dotstyle); label(" $v_4$ ", (0.2779580007834478,0.5485194236337275), NE * labelscalefactor); dot((2.558889018302256,0.660837996466093),dotstyle); label(" $v_5$ ", (2.593448579173753,0.7472368986448357), NE * labelscalefactor); clip((xmin,ymin)--(xmin,ymax)--(xmax,ymax)--(xmax,ymin)--cycle); [/asy] Note that \[\sum_{v\in N(v_i)}\Delta_{v}(v_i)=n-1,\qquad \Delta_{u}(v)+\Delta_{v}(u)=n,\qquad n-1\ge\Delta_{u}(v)\ge 1.\] Therefore, \[\Delta_{u}(v)\Delta_v(u)\ge 1\cdot (n-1)=n-1. \] We say $u\sim v$ if $u$ and $v$ are adjacent. <details><summary>Long solution</summary>We will collate together AM-GM inequalities in the following way. For each vertex  $v$ , for each of its incident edges  $(v,u_1), (v,u_2), \dots$ , we will label a positive number  $f(v,u_1), f(v,u_2), \dots$  satisfying that


- For any  $v$ ,  $\sum_{u} f(v,u) \le 1$ , where the sum goes over all vertices  $u$  adjacent to  $v$ .
- For any edge  $e = (u,v)$ ,  $f(u,v)f(v,u) \ge \frac{1}{n-1}$ .

These conditions guarantee that we can collate together two-variable AM-GMs to get the desired inequality.

Arbitrarily root the tree. The idea is that we start filling in numbers bottom-up, simultaneously starting from all the leaves at the bottom. For example, if  $a$  is a leaf connected to  $b$ , then we fill in  $f(a,b)=1$  and  $f(b,a) = \frac{1}{n-1}$ , and so on. Then a contradiction could only result at some node, if the sum of all of its existing labels is at least 1.

We prove that there is no contradiction by ``smoothing'' on the structure of the tree.**Lemma 1.**Suppose some node  $V$  in this tree has only one child. Let its father be  $U$  and let its child be  $W$ . Then if we cut off the edge  $(V,W)$  and replace it with the edge  $(U,W)$ , this makes it harder for us to fill in the numbers at  $U$ . In other words, suppose the father of  $U$  is  $U'$ , then  $f(U,U') < f(U,U')$ .

*Proof.* Suppose  $f(W,V) = a$ , then
\[f(U,V) = \frac{1}{(n-1)f(V,U)} = \frac{1}{(n-1)(1 - f(V,W))} = \frac{1}{(n-1)(1 - \frac{1}{(n-1)a})} = \frac{a}{na-a-1}.\]
If we cut off the edge  $(V,W)$  and replace it with the edge  $(U,W)$ , then the new  $f(U,V) = \frac{1}{(n-1)(V,U)} = \frac{1}{n-1}$ , and  $f(U,W) = \frac{1}{(n-1)(W,U)} = \frac{1}{(n-1)a}$ . But
\[\frac{1}{n-1} + \frac{1}{(n-1)a} = \frac{a+1}{na-a} > \frac{a}{na-a-1},\]
which means that the branch including  $V,W$  ``costs more'' than before, i.e.  $f(U,U') < f(U,U')$ .  $\square$ **Lemma 2.**Suppose all children of some node  $V$  are leaves  $W_1,\dots,W_k$ . Let the father of  $V$  be  $U$ . Then we can cut off the leaves  $W_i$  and stick them to  $U$ , and this does not make it easier for us to fill in the numbers at  $U$  (this means the same inequality as in Lemma 1).

*Proof.* The original contribution is
\[f(U,V) = \frac{1}{(n-1)f(V,U)} = \frac{1}{(n-1)(1-kf(V,W_1))} = \frac{1}{(n-1)(1-\frac{k}{n-1})} = \frac{1}{n-1-k}.\]
The contribution after we make the move is
\[(k+1)\cdot f(U,W_1) = \frac{k+1}{n-1}.\]
But clearly  $\frac{k+1}{n-1} \ge \frac{1}{n-1-k}$  when  $k \le n-2$  (which is clearly true).  $\square$ By repeatedly applying Lemma 1, we can reduce to the case where every node has at least two children or none at all. Then we repeatedly apply Lemma 2 to reduce to the case where the tree has a universal vertex, in which case the problem is clearly true.</details>

stem_md: Is it possible to write a positive integer in every cell of an infinite chessboard, in such a manner that, for all positive integers  $m, n$ , the sum of numbers in every  $m\times n$  rectangle is divisible by  $m + n$  ?
solution_md:
what
<details><summary>solution</summary>Suppose it were possible.

We first show that any two adjacent cells say  $c_1, c_2$  must in fact contain the same number. Without losing generality let us assume that  $c_1, c_2$  are in the same row. Treat that row as the number line, numbering  $c_1$  with  $1$  and  $c_2$  with  $2$ . Naturally, all cells get a number in the increasing order of  $c_1 \mapsto c_2$ . Let  $n_i$  denote the number on the cell numbered  $i$ . 

Using the interval  $[\ell, r]$  we denote the  $r-\ell+1 \times 1$  board formed by cells numbered from  $\ell$  to  $r$  in our row. Observe that using the hypotheses on  $[1, m-1]$  and  $[2, m]$  (for some positive integer  $m \geq 2$ ) we obtain that  $n_m-n_1$  is always divisible by  $m$ . By translating,  $n_x-n_y$  is always divisible by  $y-x+1$ . Suppose for the sake of contradiction that  $n_1 \ne n_2$ . Pick a prime  $p > |n_1-n_2|$ . Note that: \[n_{p+1}-n_2 \equiv n_{2p}-n_{p+1} \equiv 0 \equiv n_{2p}-n_1 \pmod p\] implying that  $p \mid n_1-n_2$ , a contradiction. 

Thus any two adjacent cells have the same number written on them, from where it follows that the whole board is constant, say at a value  $v$ . Then taking any  $1 \times n$  board, we deduce that  $n+1 \mid nv$ , or that  $n+1 \mid v$  for any positive integer  $n$ , which is impossible since  $v \ne 0$ .</details>

stem_md: Let  $\alpha , \beta , \gamma , \delta$  be positive numbers such that for all  $x$ ,  $\sin{\alpha x}+\sin {\beta x}=\sin {\gamma x}+\sin {\delta x}$ . Prove that  $\alpha =\gamma$  or  $\alpha=\delta$ .
solution_md:
The keywords are "almost periodic function". 
Let  $f(x)$  be any finite sum of complex exponentials  $\sum c_i e^{{\alpha_i}x}$ .   
The  $c_i$  and  $\alpha_i$  can be reconstructed from the set of Fourier integrals  $I_{\theta} = $  average value (on  $\mathbb{R}$ ) of  $exp (-i \theta t) f(t)$ .    $I_\theta$  is zero except when  $\theta = \alpha_i$  for some  $i$ , and the value of the integral is then the coefficient  $c_i$ .

stem_md: The inscribed sphere of a tetrahedron  $ABCD$  touches  $ABC,ABD,ACD$  and  $BCD$  at  $D_1,C_1,B_1$  and  $A_1$  respectively. Consider the plane equidistant from  $A$  and plane  $B_1C_1D_1$  (parallel to  $B_1C_1D_1$ ) and the three planes defined analogously for the vertices  $B,C,D$ . Prove that the circumcenter of the tetrahedron formed by these four planes coincides with the circumcenter of tetrahedron of  $ABCD$ .
solution_md: Let  $A'B'C'D'$  be the tetrahedron formed by the four planes. Let  $I$  be the incenter of the tetrahedron. Note that  $D'$  is the radical center of  $(A), (B), (C), \omega$ , where  $\omega$  is the incircle of the tetrahedron and  $(P)$  denotes the point-circle at  $P$ . Similar results hold for  $A', B', C'$ . Therefore, we know that  $C'D'$  is perpendicular to the plane of  $ABI$  (Carnot, say). Since  $D'A = D'B = D'C$ , if we let  $O$  be the circumcenter of  $ABCD$ , then we have that  $OD'$  is perpendicular to the plane of  $ABC$ . Similarly,  $OC'$  is perpendicular to the plane of  $ABD$ . Hence, to show that  $OC' = OD',$  we want to show that  $C'D'$  makes an equal angle with the planes of  $ABC, ABD$ . However, as  $ABI$  is the "bisector" of the planes of  $ABC, ABD$ , and  $C'D'$  is perpendicular to the plane of  $ABI$ , we're done. $\square$

stem_md: Ana and Bora are each given a sufficiently long paper strip, one with letter  $A$  written , and the other with letter  $B$ . Every minute, one of them (not necessarily one after another) writes either on the left or on the right to the word on his/her strip the word written on the other strip. Prove that the day after, one will be able to cut word on Ana's strip into two words and exchange their places, obtaining a palindromic word.
solution_md:
Solved with **magicarrow** and **tapir1729**.

Induct on the length of the number of minutes, with base cases trivial. WLOG, the words go to  $A,AB$ . Denote  $AB=B'$ , and follow the process. By inductive hypothesis, the word obtained written in terms of  $B'$ s can be split into two palindrome. Thus, it suffices to show that if a word formed from  $A$  and  $B'$  can be broken into two palindromes, then replacing all  $B'$ s with  $AB$ s maintains this property.

Indeed, applying this operation to a palindrome, we see it remains a palindrome if we either remove an  $A$  from the left, or add an  $A$  to the right. At this point, if our word split into two palindromes, we just apply the operation, and shift our divider by one to the right. This completes the proof.

So we go the "reverse" path, i.e. lets say we have a string of $A$ 's and $B$ 's such that things work, then changing $A \to AB$ and $B \to B$ or $A \to BA, B \to B$ , etc. all produce strings which can still be split up into two palindromes and we induct on the number of transformations we apply. Note that this is just playing the game in reverse effectively, where at the $n^{th}$ step of our induction we are treating our string as a string of letters where our alphabet is the strings from the $n^{th}$ minute before. Now, the base of $n=1$ is trivial. Now suppose we have made $n$ transformations and our string can be split up into $XY$ with $X,Y$ palindromes. Now we will deal with the case of $A \to AB$ , the other cases are analogous. Define $f$ as the mapping that acts on a string of letters $A,B$ and sends $A$ to $AB$ and $B$ to $B$ . Note that if $\mathcal{P}$ is a palindrome, then $Bf(\mathcal{P})$ is a palindrome by easy induction, and same with $f(\mathcal{P}) - B$ (i.e. strip a $B$ off the end). stem_md: The side lengths of a triangle are the roots of a cubic polynomial with rational coefficients. Prove that the altitudes of this triangle are roots of a polynomial of sixth degree with rational coefficients.
solution_md:
This problem is not as daunting as it may seem. 

Suppose  $r_1, r_2, r_3$  are roots of some cubic  $ax^3 + bx^2 + cx + d$ . Then we have that by Vieta,  $r_1 + r_2 + r_3 = \frac{-b}{a} \in \mathbb{Q}$ , and  $r_1r_2 + r_2r_3 + r_3r_1 = \frac{c}{a} \in \mathbb{Q}$ , and finally  $r_1r_2r_3 = -d/a \in \mathbb{Q}$ . Hence each  $r_i, 1 \leq i \leq 3$  is rational also. 

Note that the altitudes are given by  $2[\text{area}]/r_i$ . Now the area is simply  $\sqrt{s(s - r_1)(s - r_2)(s - r_3)}$ , where  $s$  is the semiperimeter (this is due to Heron's formula). Now for simplicity, let  $X = \sqrt{s(s - r_1)(s - r_2)(s - r_3)}$ . Consider the polynomial \[\left(x^2 - \frac{4X^2}{r_1^2}\right) \left(x^2 - \frac{4X^2}{r_2^2} \right) \left(x^2 - \frac{4X^2}{r_3^2} \right). \] Here each  $\frac{4X^2}{r_i^2}$  is clearly rational. Hence this new polynomial will have rational coefficients, and also have degree  $6$ .  $\blacksquare$

stem_md: Is there a natural number   $ n > 10^{1000}$  which is not divisible by 10 and which satisfies: in its decimal representation one can exchange two distinct non-zero digits such that the set of prime divisors does not change.
solution_md:
Clearly this is the only way to prove it:
Consider the  $2$  numbers as:  $\prod{p_i ^{a_i+b_i}}$  and  $\prod{p_i ^{a_i+c_i}}$  with all  $a_i \geq 1$ ,  $b_i, c_i \geq 0$ , and for each  $i$  one of  $b_i, c_i$  is  $0$  but not all of them are  $0$ : $10^k$   $<$   $\prod{p_i ^{a_i+c_i}}$    $<$   $\prod{p_i ^{a_i+b_i}}$    $<$   $10^{k+1}$ , with  $k \geq 1000$ .
The difference is: $\prod{p_i ^{a_i}}(\prod{p_i ^{b_i}}-\prod{p_i ^{c_i}})=d(10^m-1)10^n$ , with  $d \in $ { $1,2,...,8$ },  $m \geq 1$ ,  $n \geq 0$ .
Also we have  $\prod{p_i ^{c_i}}$   $<$   $\prod{p_i ^{b_i}}$   $<$   $9 \prod{p_i ^{c_i}}$ , then get some contradiction.

stem_md: Let  $n > 3$  be a natural number, and let  $x_1$ ,  $x_2$ , ...,  $x_n$  be  $n$  positive real numbers whose product is  $1$ . Prove the inequality \[ \frac {1}{1 + x_1 + x_1\cdot x_2} + \frac {1}{1 + x_2 + x_2\cdot x_3} + ... + \frac {1}{1 + x_n + x_n\cdot x_1} > 1. \]
solution_md:
Let $ f(x_1,x_2,...,x_n)$ be our expression. It's easy to see that for $ n = 3$ , the expression is exactly equal to 1, because it is $ \dsp \frac {1}{1 + x_2 + x_2x_3}(\frac {1}{x_1} + 1 + x_2) = 1$ . Now, prove it by induction over $ n$ . We will always find one of the $ x_i$ 's $ \geq$ than 1 such that $ x_i \cdot x_{i + 1} \geq 1$ . If there weren't such an $ x_i$ , then the product of the numbers would obviously be < 1. So if $ x_i > 1$ and $ x_i \cdot x_{i + 1} \geq 1$ , it's easy to see that $ f(x_1,x_2,...,x_n) > f(x_1,...,x_{i - 2},x_{i - 1}\cdot x_{i},x_{i + 1},...,x_n)$ , because \[ \dsp \frac {1}{1 + x_{i - 2} + x_{i - 2}x_{i - 1}} + \frac {1}{1 + x_{i - 1} + x_{i - 1}x_i} + \frac {1}{1 + x_i + x_ix_{i + 1}} > \frac {1}{1 + x_{i - 2} + x_{i - 2}x_{i - 1}x_i} + \frac {1}{1 + x_{i - 1}x_i + x_{i - 1}x_ix_{i + 1}}\] This is true because the first two terms in LHS are greater than the first two terms on RHS. So our induction is complete.

Each grid point of a cartesian plane is colored with one of three colors, whereby all three colors are used. Show that one can always find a right-angled triangle, whose three vertices have pairwise different colors.
**Solution:** Suppose there exists a line $\ell$ with point $X_1,X_2,X_3$ in the same order and have the colour $C_1,C_2,C_3$ . Let $\ell_i$ be the perpendicular line to $\ell$ at $X_i$ . Note that, every point on line $\ell_i$ must have the colour $C_i$ , otherwise we readily have the triangle. Name $X_2$ as $A$ . Choose point $B$ on $\ell_1$ and $C$ on $\ell_3$ . Let $x,y$ be distances $X_1X_2$ and $X_2X_3$ . Let $B'$ be foot from $B$ to $\ell_3$ and Let $k,m$ be distances $BX_1$ and $B'C$ (WLOG, assume, $X_3C$ $>$ $X_1B$ ). Choose $k,m$ such that $xy$ $=$ $k(k+m)$ . We can obviously find such $k,m$ when $xy>1$ and the construction is obvious when $xy=1$ , thus by Pythagoras' Theorem, $AB^2$ $+$ $AC^2$ $=$ $BC^2$ . Now, We'll show that such a configuration, where $3$ points with different colour on the same line exists. Take a line $\ell$ with all points on it having colour $C_1$ . Let $A,B$ be a points having colour $C_2$ , $C_3$ . Consider the intersection of perpendicular from $B$ to $\ell$ and parallel to $\ell$ through $A$ . Clearly this point must have the colour $C_2$ otherwise we're done and thus we arrive at the configuration. Suppose there exists a line $\ell$ with all points having colour $C_1$ and a point $A$ with colour $C_2$ . Take point $B$ with colour $C_3$ and notice that the intersection of perpendicular from $B$ to $\ell$ must have colour $C_3$ otherwise we're done and thus we again arrive at our required configuration $\qquad \blacksquare$

Then, the line  $x = c$  for any integer  $c$  intersects  $y = 0$  at  $(c, 0)$ , so since the line  $x = c$  is monochromatic, it must also be all red. This implies that  $\mathbb{Z}^2$  is all red since any  $(a, b) \in \mathbb{Z}^2$  lies on  $x = a$ , which is all red, contradicting the fact that all colors are used at least once. 

Thus, there exists a line with at least two colors. WLOG let those colors be red and blue, and WLOG 
let the line be  $y = 0$ . Let the coordinate of the red point be  $P_1 = (a, 0)$  and let the coordinate of the blue point be  $P_2 = (b, 0)$ . Then, there exists a green point  $Q = (c, d)\in \mathbb{Z}^2$ . Then, let  $P_3 = (a, d)$  and  $P_4 = (b, d)$ . Then,  $P_3$  is red, since if  $P_3$  was blue, then  $\triangle P_1P_3Q$  would be right and its vertices would all be pairwise different colors,  and if  $P_3$  was green, then  $\triangle P_3P_1P_2$  would be right and its vertices would all be pairwise different colors. Similarly, we can show that  $P_2$  is blue. Then, it follows that  $Q\notin \{P_3, P_4\}$ , and the line  $y = d$  contains three points  $P_3, P_4, Q$  of pairwise distinct colors. Now, this means that the whole line  $x = a$  is red, since if a point  $A$  on it was blue, then  $\triangle AP_3Q$  is a right triangle with vertices all pairwise different colors, and if  $A$  was green, then  $\triangle AP_3P_4$  is a right triangle with all vertices pairwise different colors. Similarly, the whole line  $x = b$  is blue and the whole line  $x = c$  is is green. Then, if  $Q_3 = (b, d+b-a)$  and  $R_3 = (c, d+a-c)$ , then the slope of  $P_3Q_3$  is   $$ \frac{(d+b-a) - d}{b-a} = 1, $$   and the slope of  $P_3R_3$  is   $$ \frac{(d+a-c) - d}{c-a} = -1, $$   and these multiply to  $-1$ , so it follows that  $\angle Q_3P_3R_3 = 90^{\circ}$ , so  $\triangle P_3Q_3R_3$  is right. The exterior angle bisectors of the angles  $DAB$  and  $ABC$  intersect each other at  $K$ ; the exterior angle bisectors of the angles  $ABC$  and  $BCD$  intersect each other at  $L$ ; the exterior angle bisectors of the angles  $BCD$  and  $CDA$  intersect each other at  $M$ ; the exterior angle bisectors of the angles  $CDA$  and  $DAB$  intersect each other at  $N$ . Let  $K_{1}$ ,  $L_{1}$ ,  $M_{1}$  and  $N_{1}$  be the orthocenters of the triangles  $ABK$ ,  $BCL$ ,  $CDM$  and  $DAN$ , respectively. Show that the quadrilateral  $K_{1}L_{1}M_{1}N_{1}$  is a parallelogram.
solution_md:
This seems to be one of the easier Russian problems, so let's get it out of the way :).

Let  $I$  be the incenter of  $ABCD$ .  $I$  is also the intersection pt of the bisectors of  $ABCD$ , so  $AI \perp AK \Rightarrow BK_1||AI$ . In the same way we get  $AK_1||BI$ , so if we let  $I$  be the origin of the plane and work with complex numbers, we get  $k_1=a+b$ . 

After writing down the similar relations, we find  $k_1+m_1=l_1+n_1 (=a+b+c+d)$ , and this is the necessary and sufficient condition for  $K_1L_1M_1N_1$  to be a parallelogram.

stem_md: On a table there are 2004 boxes, and in each box a ball lies. I know that some the balls are white and that the number of white balls is even. In each case I may point to two arbitrary boxes and ask whether in the box contains at least a white ball lies. After which minimum number of questions I can indicate two boxes for sure, in which white balls lie?
solution_md:
Reworded for clarity.
There are $2004$ boxes, each containing a white or a black ball. It is known that a non-zero even number of balls are white. A move consists of picking two boxes and asking whether at least one of them contains a white ball. What minimal number of questions is required, after which one can indicate two boxes both containing a white ball?
I claim that $4005$ is the desired minimum. Consider this as a game played by two players, *Fate* and *Hope,* where *Hope* asks the questions and *Fate* replies to them truthfully with a "yes" or a "no". For convenience, identify the boxes by the color of the balls they contain.**Strategy for Hope:** Label the boxes as $1,2, \dots, 2004$ and ask questions of the form $(1, i), (1,2), (2,i)$ for all $3 \le i \le 2004$ . For the first $2003$ questions, if any of them is answered by a "no" then we get $1$ is black; so all the "yes" answers tell us exactly which balls are white, and we are done. Now, assume they were all answered by a "yes". If $1$ is black then some other index in $\{2,3,\dots, 2004\}$ is also black as there are an even number of black indices; so $1$ must be white. If any of the next $2002$ questions is answered by a "no" then we know that $2$ is black and exactly which of $\{3, \dots, 2004\}$ are white by looking at the "yes" answers. If all are "yes" then $2$ cannot be black since the set $\{2,3, \dots, 2004\}$ contains an even number of black indices. Evidently, we can identify $1,2$ as white. Thus, the strategy indeed works.**Strategy for Fate:** Suppose *Hope* has a strategy which allows her a win in $m \le 4004$ questions regardless of what *Fate* does. *Fate's* strategy now is to say "yes" to all questions. We can assume, in this case, that *Hope's* strategy is independent of the feedback she receives; simply because all the answers she receives will be "yes". It is sufficient to show that there exists a coloring of the boxes for which these answers are consistent but *Hope's* strategy fails. Following her strategy; suppose she indicates two boxes $A$ and $B$ at last. If $A, B$ were not inquired about before; then we can color $A, B$ as black and all other balls as white. If $A, B$ were inquired about before, then, say there exists a box $C$ which is not questioned with at least one of $A, B$ . WLOG, let it be $A$ ; then color $A, C$ as black and all other boxes as white. Such a vertex $C$ exists otherwise we have at least $1+2002+2002=4005$ questions asked. Hence, *Hope's* strategy does not necessarily work for $m \le 4004$ questions.

stem_md: Are there such pairwise distinct natural numbers  $ m, n, p, q$  satisfying  $ m \plus{} n \equal{} p \plus{} q$  and  $ \sqrt{m} \plus{} \sqrt[3]{n} \equal{} \sqrt{p} \plus{} \sqrt[3]{q} > 2004$  ?
solution_md:
Let  $ n\equal{}b^3$ ,  $ q\equal{}a^3$ , then  $ m\equal{}k\minus{}b^3$ ,  $ n\equal{}k\minus{}a^3$  and we have to find a solution to $ \sqrt{k\minus{}b^3}\plus{}b\equal{}\sqrt{k\minus{}a^3}\plus{}a$ 
Let  $ k\equal{}b^3\plus{}y^2$ , then  $ m\equal{}y^2$ , we have to solve $ y\plus{}b\equal{}\sqrt{b^3\plus{}y^2\minus{}a^3}\plus{}a$  $ (y\plus{}b\minus{}a)^2\equal{}b^3\plus{}y^2\minus{}a^3$  $ (b\minus{}a)(b\minus{}a\plus{}2y)\equal{}(b\minus{}a)(b^2\plus{}ab\plus{}a^2)$  $ 2y\equal{}a^2\plus{}b^2\plus{}ab\plus{}a\minus{}b$ 
Let  $ a\equal{}2r$ ,  $ b\equal{}2$ . Then  $ y\equal{}2r^2\plus{}3r\plus{}1$ 
So  $ n\equal{}8$ ,  $ q\equal{}8r^3$ ,  $ m\equal{}4r^4\plus{}12r^3\plus{}13r^2\plus{}6r\plus{}1\equal{}(2r^2\plus{}3r\plus{}1)^2$ ,  $ p\equal{}4r^4\plus{}4r^3\plus{}13r^2\plus{}6r\plus{}9\equal{}(2r^2\plus{}r\plus{}3)^2$ 
And we can make  $ r$  arbitrarily large.

stem_md: In the cabinet 2004 telephones are located; each two of these telephones are connected by a cable, which is colored in one of four colors. From each color there is one cable at least. Can one always select several telephones in such a way that among their pairwise cable connections exactly 3 different colors occur?
solution_md:
I wonder that nobody can solve this problem! It's rather easy one, I suppose.

Answer: yes.

We will consider not telephones but respective graph  $G$ . Suppose there exist a vertex  $u$  s.t. the edges of the graph  $G \setminus \{u\}$  are colored in 4 colors. Then we will delete this vertex. And then we will continue deleting vertices with preserving 4 colors. We will do it until we can't do it. Then it is easy to see that deleting any vertex implies disapearing at least 2 colors (if for some vertex only one color disapears then we are done). It means that there exist a vertex  $u$  s.t. all blue edges and all red edges incident to the vertex  $u$  (for some colors "blue" and "red"). Let  $uv$  be blue edge and  $uw$  be red edge. But then the edge  $vw$  can't be blue or red, since it doesn't incident to  $u$ . Hence the set  $(u,v,w)$  is desired. The problem is completely solved.

Suppose there are exactly 50 good pairs. Without loss of generality we may assume that $(a_1,a_2)$ , $(a_3,a_4)$ , ..., $(a_{99},a_{100})$ are good pairs and $a_1a_3<\ldots>a_{99}a_1$ . stem_md: A country has 1001 cities, and each two cities are connected by a one-way street. From each city exactly 500 roads begin, and in each city 500 roads end. Now an independent republic splits itself off the country, which contains 668 of the 1001 cities. Prove that one can reach every other city of the republic from each city of this republic without being forced to leave the republic.
solution_md:
For all cities  $X$  in the republic, let us greedily determine all other cities in the republic reachable from that city, denoted as the set  $N(X).$  

Without loss of generality, suppose that there exist two cities  $A$  and  $B$  within the republic such that  $N(A)$  and  $N(B)$  are disjoint. I proceed by double-counting the sum of the out-degrees of the cities in  $N(A)$  and the sum of the out-degrees of the cities in  $N(B),$  within the republic. 

Firstly, if some city in  $N(A)$  can reach some city in the republic not in  $N(A),$  then  $N(A)$  would not be a complete set of cities reachable from  $A,$  contradiction. Therefore, the sum of the out-degrees is upper-bounded by:   $$ \sum_{X \in N(A)} \text{outdeg}(X) \le \binom{|N(A)|}{2}. $$   On the other hand, given any  $X \in N(A),$  there are at most  $332$  possible cities outside of the republic that  $X$  can lead to, so the minimum out-degree of  $X$  within the republic is   $$ 500-332-1=167. $$   Therefore, the sum of the out-degrees is lower-bounded by:   $$ \sum_{X \in N(A)} \text{outdeg}(X) \ge 167|N(A)|. $$   It results that   $$ \binom{|N(A)|}{2} \ge 167|N(A)| \implies |N(A)| \ge 335. $$   Analogously, we have  $|N(B)| \ge 335.$  

However, by the Pigeonhole Principle, it results that
\begin{align*}
    |N(A) \cap N(B)| &= |N(A)|+|N(B)|-|N(A) \cup N(B)| 
    &\ge 335+335-668 
    &= 2 
    &> 0,
\end{align*}
contradiction. 

Hence, our original assumption that there exist two cities  $A$  and  $B$  in the republic which are not reachable from each other must have been false, concluding the proof.  $\square$

Repeating the same argument for the indegree of vertices in  $|X_v|$ , we get similarly 
\[ 500 \ge |Y_v| + \frac{|X_v|-1}{2}. \]
Adding these two, we get  $1000\ge \tfrac32|X_v|+\tfrac32|Y_v|-1$ , so  $|X_v|+|Y_v| \le \tfrac23 \cdot 1001 = 667\tfrac13$ . But  $|X_v|+|Y_v|=668$ , contradiction. Therefore,  $|X_v|=0$  or  $|Y_v|=0$ . But  $|X_v|\ge 1$  since  $v\in X_v$ . Hence  $|Y_v|=0$ , and we are done.

stem_md: A triangle  $ T$  is contained inside a point-symmetrical polygon  $ M.$  The triangle  $ T'$  is the mirror image of the triangle  $ T$  with the reflection at one point  $ P$ , which inside the triangle  $ T$  lies. Prove that at least one of the vertices of the triangle  $ T'$  lies in inside or on the boundary of the polygon  $ M.$
solution_md:
Indeed I have just looked at the official ARO 2004 brochure. Amfulger and Myth are right: The polygon M must be convex. Actually, the official brochure gives two solutions of the problem; the first one implicitely uses the convexity of M, while the second one explicitely says "Since M is convex, [...]". Inspite of this, there is no mention of the convexity in the statement of the problem. Hence I propose to rewrite the problem statement as follows:

*Let T be a triangle lying completely inside a point-symmetrical convex polygon M. Let T' be the reflection of the triangle T in an arbitrary point P which lies inside the triangle T. Prove that at least one of the vertices of the triangle T' lies inside or on the boundary of the polygon M.*

Here is the *first solution* from the brochure:

Let O be the center of symmetry of the polygon M; let A, B, C be the vertices of the triangle T, and let A', B', C' be the corresponding vertices of the triangle T'. In other words, the points A', B', C' are the reflections of the points A, B, C in the point P. Since the polygon M is point-symmetric with respect to the point O, the reflections X, Y, Z of the points A, B, C in the point O all lie inside M. If O = P, then X = A', Y = B' and Z = C', so that everything is trivial. Hence, the only case we need to consider is when  $O\neq P$ . Then, let d be the ray which falls along the line OP but begins at the point P and doesn't contain the point O. Then, since the point P lies inside triangle ABC, this ray d intersects one of the sides of triangle ABC. Assume WLOG that this side is the side AB. Let the ray d intersect the side AB at a point U.

Then, of course, since the point U lies on the ray d, the point P lies between the points U and O. Denoting by V and K the reflections of this point U in the points O and P, respectively, it clearly follows that the point K lies between the points U and V (since the points U, K and V are just the images of the points U, P and O in the homothety with center U and factor 2).

Since the points X, Y and V are the reflections of the points A, B and U in the point O, from the fact that the point U lies on the segment AB, it follows that the point V lies on the segment XY. Similarly, since the points A', B' and K are the reflections of the points A, B and U in the point P, from the fact that the point U lies on the segment AB, it follows that the point K lies on the segment A'B'.

Now, since the points X and Y are the reflections of the points A and B in the point O, the quadrilateral ABXY is a parallelogram with center O. This parallelogram completely lies inside the polygon M (since M is convex, and the points A, B, X, Y lie inside M). The points U and V lie on the sides AB and XY of this parallelogram, and the point K, which - as we know - lies between the points U and V, must therefore lie inside this parallelogram. Now, this point K lies on the segment A'B'; thus, the segment A'B' has a common point with the parallelogram ABXY. But as the points A' and B' are the reflections of the points A and B in the point P, the segment A'B' is parallel and equal to the segment AB; thus, since this segment A'B' has a common point with the parallelogram ABXY, one of the endpoints A' and B' of this segment must lie inside or on the boundary of the parallelogram ABXY (else, the segment A'B' would cross through the parallelogram - i. e. enter it on one side and quit it again on the other side -, but then its length would be > AB). We can WLOG assume that the point A' lies inside or on the boundary of the parallelogram ABXY. Since the parallelogram ABXY itself lies inside the polygon M, it follows that the point A' lies inside the polygon M. Hence, we have found a vertex of the triangle T' which lies inside the polygon M; the problem is solved.

  Darij

stem_md: The polynomials  $ P(x)$  and  $ Q(x)$  are given. It is known that for a certain polynomial  $ R(x, y)$  the identity  $ P(x) \minus{} P(y) \equal{} R(x, y) (Q(x) \minus{} Q(y))$  applies. Prove that there is a polynomial  $ S(x)$  so that  $ P(x) \equal{} S(Q(x)) \quad \forall x.$
solution_md:
We have $Q(x)-Q(y) \mid P(x)-P(y)$ . Use the Division Algorithm to write $P(x)=A(x)Q(x) + B(x)$ for some $A,B\in \mathbb{R}[x]$ with $\deg B < \deg Q$ . We have \[ Q(x)-Q(y) \mid \big[A(x)Q(x)-A(y)Q(y) \big]+\big[B(x)-B(y)\big] \qquad (\clubsuit). \] Let $\{r_1,\ldots,r_k\}$ be the set of distinct roots of $Q$ , and let $Q(x) = (x-r_1)^{a_1}\cdots (x-r_k)^{a_k}$ for some $(a_i) \in \mathbb{Z}_{\ge 1}$ . If $r$ and $s$ are roots of $Q$ , then plugging in $x=r$ and $y=s$ above implies $B(r)=B(s)$ . Hence $B(r_1)=\cdots=B(r_k)$ . Therefore, \[ B(x)-c = (x-r_1)^{b_1}\cdots (x-r_k)^{b_k} \qquad (\spadesuit)\] for some constant $c\in \mathbb{R}$ and for some $(b_i)\in \mathbb{Z}_{\ge 1}$ . ----------------------- From $(\clubsuit)$ , we get \[ Q(x)-Q(y) \mid \big[A(x)-A(y) \big]Q(x) +\big[B(x)-B(y)\big]. \] We know $x-y\mid P(x)-P(y)$ for any polynomial $P$ . Hence we can write -- as a polynomial statement -- the following: \[ \frac{Q(x)-Q(y)}{x-y} \Biggr| \left[ \frac{A(x)-A(y)}{x-y} \right ]Q(x) +\left[\frac{B(x)-B(y)}{x-y}\right]. \] Taking the limit as $y$ approaches $x$ , the above implies \[ Q'(x) \mid A'(x)Q(x) + B'(x) \implies A'(x)Q(x)+B'(x) = Q'(x)S(x,y) \qquad (\heartsuit)\] for some $S(x,y) \in \mathbb{R}[x,y]$ . ---------------------- **Lemma:**If $Q$ has a root $r$ with multiplicity $n$ , then $r$ is also a root of $B$ , and it has multiplicity at least $n$ . *Proof:* Replace $n$ with $n+1$ . We know $Q(r)=0$ and $Q'(r)=0$ , and so on till $Q^{(n)}(r)=0$ . Taking $n-1$ derivatives of $(\heartsuit)$ , every term on the LHS (except $B^{(n)}(x)$ ) and every term on the RHS will have a term $Q^{(m)}(x)$ for some $m\in \{0,\ldots,n\}$ , and is hence $0$ . Therefore, $B^{(n)}(x)=0$ , and also by the same logic $B^{(m)}(x)=0$ for any $m \le n$ . Therefore, $B$ has a root at $r$ with multiplicity $n$ as well. $\blacksquare$ **Claim:** $B(x)$ is a constant polynomial. *Proof:* Suppose $Q$ has a root $r_i$ with multiplicity $a_i\ge 2$ . By the Lemma, so does $b$ , so $(x-r_i)^{a_i} \mid B(x)$ . Hence $B'(x)$ has a root at $r_i$ with multiplicity at least $a_i-1$ . By $(\spadesuit)$ , $B'(x)$ has a root at $r_i$ with multiplicity $b_i-1$ . Therefore, $b_i-1\ge a_i-1$ , so $b_i\ge a_i$ . Summing over all $i$ , we get $\deg B \ge \deg Q$ , contradiction. Therefore, we must have $B(x)=c$ in fact, since the $0$ polynomial has any number as a root, and any root has infinite multiplicity. $\blacksquare$ -------------------- Now we are almost done. We claim $A(x)$ also works in the place of $P(x)$ in the original statement. Indeed, since $P(x)=A(x)Q(x)+c$ , and $Q(x)-Q(y) \mid P(x)-P(y)$ , we have $Q(x)-Q(y) \mid A(x)Q(x)-A(y)Q(y)$ , which implies $Q(x)-Q(y) \mid [A(x)-A(y)]Q(x)$ . But $\gcd(Q(x),Q(x)-Q(y)) = \gcd(Q(x),Q(y))=1$ since they are polynomials purely in different variables. Therefore, $Q(x)-Q(y)\mid A(x)-A(y)$ , as claimed. Now we can continue the process, and backtracking once the process is finished, we get that $P(x)$ is a polynomial in $Q(x)$ (the process essentially builds up the polynomial in $Q$ , increasing the degree by $1$ at each step).
RemarksThe main ideas and motivation of the solution are: - Writing $P=AQ+B$ using Division Algorithm. This is motivated since the final result of the problem is that we want to show $P$ is a polynomial in $Q$ , so we want to ``build up'' $P$ in terms of $Q$ , motivating using Division Algorithm. We want to show $B$ is a constant. - After manipulating the above into $(\clubsuit)$ , the idea is to plug in $r$ and $s$ if they are two roots of $Q$ -- this gets rid of everything except $B(r)-B(s)$ , so it is also $0$ . From here, we have that the set of roots of $B$ (translated by a constant) and $Q$ is the same. This is a pretty key step, and a trick the problem uses a lot -- vanish a lot of stuff so the remaining stuff is also $0$ . - Now that the set of roots is the same, the hard part of the problem is dealing with multiplicity. The best way to deal with multiplicity in general is through derivatives. We get $Q' \mid A'Q+B'$ after some trickery. We need to use the fact that $\deg Q > \deg B$ , and using $(\heartsuit)$ , we can prove that the multiplicities of the roots of $B$ and $Q$ are the same; not just that they have the same set of roots. Now we are basically done.
